expected_output.reasoning:
The expected root cause is that the discrepancy is located on the client side of the measurement boundary—CloudWatch InvocationLatency only measures service-side time, and the app-side latency gap is due to something outside Bedrock's inference path (e.g., connection setup, client init, etc.).

The investigation's root cause finding precisely matches this: "Recreated Lambdas ran 100% cold, and per-invocation Bedrock client setup inflated each cold start." It explicitly identifies that the Lambda functions were recreated on 11-16, causing 100% cold starts, and that the handlers build the boto3 bedrock-runtime client inside the handler, so cold starts pay for SDK loading, credential/endpoint resolution, and first TLS connection — all client-side overhead that happens "before the request reaches Bedrock, so AWS/Bedrock InvocationLatency never records it."

The investigation also explicitly validates that Bedrock latency did not regress at the service level (improved week over week, no throttles/errors), and identifies the telemetry gap (LLM-TEL-001) that the app logs only total handler time, conflating cold-start/client-init overhead with model latency, explaining the measurement-boundary mismatch with CloudWatch.

This aligns closely with the expected root cause: the cause is on the client side (Lambda cold start + client init overhead), outside Bedrock's own inference path, and the measurement-boundary discrepancy (CloudWatch only measures service-side) is identified as decisive evidence. The investigation goes further to pinpoint the specific client-side mechanism (Lambda redeploy causing cold starts + in-handler client construction), which is consistent with and more specific than the expected answer's general description of "connection setup" as one of the possible client-side causes.

This is a strong match - same underlying conclusion that the latency increase originates outside Bedrock's measured inference path, on the client/application side.
